High school academics

Summary
Big takeaway:
High school academic indicators matter, but none are strong predictors of workforce outcomes on their own. Across all academic measures, the relationships are consistent, statistically significant, and substantively modest. Academic experiences shape risk gradients, not deterministic pathways, and their influence is already visible in year 1 and remains stable through year 5.
Standardized Test Performance (ACT, MCA Math, Reading, Science)
Across all four assessments, higher scores are consistently associated with better workforce attachment, and lower scores with higher likelihood of disconnection—especially No Minnesota employment record. However, effect sizes are small (Cramer’s V ≈ 0.04–0.12), indicating broad overlap across categories.

ACT Composite Score shows the strongest academic signal:

Individuals with No MN employment record have ACT scores roughly 1–1.7 points higher than those in meaningful in-region employment, reflecting selection into test-taking and postsecondary exposure rather than pure academic skill.
Differences between meaningful employment categories are modest and stable across years.

MCA Math, Reading, and Science:

Higher proficiency levels (3–4) are modestly overrepresented in meaningful employment, especially statewide MN employment.
Lower proficiency levels (1–2) are more common among No MN employment record and marginal employment categories.
All MCA subjects exhibit very weak but persistent associations, with no strengthening or decay over time.


Postsecondary Exposure Signals (PSEO, Took ACT)

Took ACT is one of the clearer academic markers:

ACT takers are consistently less likely to have No MN employment records and more likely to be meaningfully employed.
Effect sizes are modest but stronger than most other academic indicators and stable across all five years.

PSEO participation shows a similar but slightly weaker pattern:

Participants are more likely to be meaningfully employed and less likely to be fully detached.
Differences are present in year 1 and persist, suggesting early sorting rather than later divergence.


Career & Technical Education (CTE)
CTE engagement shows consistent protective effects, particularly against full detachment.

CTE Concentrators/Completers are:

More likely to be in meaningful in-region or MN employment
Less likely to have No MN employment record

No CTE students are overrepresented among disconnected categories across all years.
Number of CTE courses taken:

Individuals in meaningful employment average ~0.25–0.55 more CTE courses than those with no MN employment record.
Differences are statistically significant but modest and stable over time.


Interpretation Across the Academic Block
Taken together, high school academics function as risk modifiers, not sorting mechanisms. Stronger academic preparation, postsecondary signaling (ACT, PSEO), and CTE engagement all reduce the likelihood of complete labor force detachment, but none sharply separate marginal from stable employment.
Crucially, these academic effects are: - Visible immediately after exit - Stable across five years - Weaker than postsecondary attendance effects - Stronger than county-level economic conditions
This reinforces a central conclusion of the broader analysis:
Persistent workforce disconnection is not primarily an academic failure problem, but academic experiences can meaningfully buffer against the worst outcomes, especially full detachment from Minnesota’s labor market.

Participation in PSEO shows a modest but consistent association with workforce outcomes across the first five years after exit from formal education. The relationship is strongest in the first year after exit and weakens slightly over time, though it remains statistically detectable in every year.
Across all five years, individuals who participated in PSEO are less likely to have no Minnesota employment record and more likely to be in meaningful employment, particularly statewide meaningful employment, compared to those who did not participate. Differences in in-region meaningful employment are smaller, suggesting that PSEO participation is more strongly associated with continued labor force attachment and mobility than with strictly local employment.
PSEO participants are also consistently less concentrated in marginal in-region employment, especially in the early post-exit years. Over time, the gap narrows somewhat, indicating that non-PSEO participants gradually improve their workforce attachment, but do not fully close the gap.
Overall, PSEO participation functions as an early protective factor against labor force detachment. Its influence appears strongest during the initial transition out of formal education and stabilizes at a lower level in later years, suggesting that early exposure to postsecondary environments helps reduce the risk of immediate disconnection, even among individuals who ultimately do not complete a college credential.

ACT participation shows a moderate and persistent relationship with workforce outcomes across all five years after exit from formal education. Unlike PSEO, where effects are strongest early and then attenuate slightly, the association between taking the ACT and workforce outcomes remains stable and even strengthens modestly by year five.
Across every year, individuals who took the ACT are substantially more likely to be in meaningful employment, particularly statewide meaningful employment, and consistently less likely to have no Minnesota employment record. By year five, the gap in full labor force detachment between ACT-takers and non-takers is pronounced, indicating that ACT participation is strongly associated with sustained workforce attachment rather than only short-term advantages.
Differences in marginal in-region employment and other disconnected employment are present but secondary. The primary distinction driven by ACT participation is between being connected to the Minnesota labor market at all versus falling completely out of it.
Importantly, these patterns persist even though ACT participation is not itself a credential. This suggests that taking the ACT functions as a signal of academic engagement, planning, or institutional connection, rather than simply reflecting test performance. ACT participation appears to mark individuals who are better positioned to navigate early workforce transitions, even when they do not complete postsecondary education.
Overall, ACT participation emerges as a stronger and more durable predictor of workforce outcomes than PSEO participation and substantially stronger than place-based high school characteristics, reinforcing the importance of engagement and signaling behaviors during high school.

CTE achievement shows a consistent and stable association with workforce outcomes across all five years after exit from formal education. While effect sizes are modest, they are uniform across time, indicating that the relationship between CTE engagement and workforce outcomes neither fades nor intensifies as individuals move further from educational exit.
Across every year, individuals who are CTE concentrators or completers are more likely to be in meaningful employment, particularly in-region employment, and less likely to have no Minnesota employment record, compared to individuals with no CTE experience. CTE participants (who did not reach concentrator or completer status) consistently fall between these two groups, reinforcing a clear dose–response pattern: deeper engagement in CTE is associated with stronger workforce attachment.
Differences between CTE groups are most pronounced in full labor force detachment, with individuals who have no CTE experience consistently overrepresented in the No Minnesota employment record category. In contrast, differences in marginal in-region employment are smaller, suggesting that CTE achievement primarily affects whether individuals remain connected to the labor force at all, rather than only job quality among those already employed.
Overall, CTE achievement functions as a durable protective factor against labor force detachment. Although its independent explanatory power is smaller than that of ACT participation or special education status, its stability across time and clear gradient by level of engagement make it one of the most policy-relevant high school academic variables in the analysis.

(Approximately 0.7–0.8% of total variance in CTE course-taking is explained by workforce category across years.)
Across all five years after exiting formal education, total CTE courses taken shows a consistent and statistically significant relationship with workforce outcomes. While the overall share of variance explained is modest, it is substantially larger and more meaningful than that observed for county-level labor market conditions.
In every year, individuals in Meaningful employment (especially in-region) completed the highest average number of CTE courses in high school. Those in Meaningful MN employment generally follow closely behind. Individuals in Not meaningful employment completed fewer CTE courses, and those with No Minnesota employment record consistently show the lowest CTE course counts.
Pairwise comparisons reinforce a clear gradient: the largest and most consistent gaps occur between Meaningful employment groups and the No MN employment record group, with differences on the order of 0.4–0.6 fewer CTE courses. Differences between the two meaningful employment groups are smaller and sometimes not statistically significant, while gaps among disconnected categories are less consistent.
Importantly, this pattern is remarkably stable over time. The ordering of group means does not change as individuals move further from educational exit, indicating that depth of CTE exposure is associated with sustained workforce attachment, not just short-term placement.
Overall, these results suggest that the number of CTE courses taken—beyond simple participation—matters for long-run workforce outcomes. CTE depth appears to function as a durable protective factor against labor force detachment, distinguishing stable employment trajectories from marginal and disconnected ones in ways that local labor market conditions do not.

ACT Composite Score shows a consistent and meaningful relationship with workforce outcomes across all five years after exiting formal education. Unlike county labor market measures, ACT scores clearly differentiate workforce categories, and this differentiation remains stable over time.
Across every year, individuals with No Minnesota employment record have the highest average ACT scores, followed by those in Not meaningful employment (other) and Not meaningful in-region employment. Individuals in Meaningful in-region employment consistently have the lowest average ACT scores, with those in Meaningful employment in Minnesota falling in between.
The magnitude of differences is substantive: gaps of roughly 1.0–1.7 ACT points separate meaningful in-region employment from no-MN-record individuals in every year. These differences are statistically significant and persistent, indicating that academic preparation—as measured by ACT performance—is strongly linked to where and how individuals attach to the workforce after leaving education.
Importantly, higher ACT scores do not correspond to stronger local attachment. Instead, higher scorers are more likely to be absent from Minnesota employment records or in employment that does not register as meaningful locally. This suggests that academic achievement is associated with greater mobility and exit from local labor markets, rather than protection against labor force disconnection within the region.
Overall, ACT performance is one of the strongest individual-level predictors examined so far in distinguishing post-education workforce pathways, particularly in separating locally attached employment from external or non-recorded employment trajectories.

MCA Math performance shows a statistically significant but weak and highly stable relationship with workforce outcomes across all five years after exiting formal education. Cramer’s V values remain consistently in the 0.04–0.06 range, indicating that math achievement explains only a small share of variation in early workforce trajectories.
Across all years, higher MCA Math scores (Levels 3–4) are modestly associated with higher shares of meaningful employment, particularly in-region and statewide Minnesota employment. Conversely, lower scores (Levels 1–2) are associated with slightly higher representation in No Minnesota employment records and other disconnected categories. However, these differences are incremental rather than decisive.
Importantly, the relationship does not strengthen or weaken over time. The influence of MCA Math achievement on workforce category placement appears largely front-loaded and stable, with no evidence that math proficiency becomes more predictive as individuals move further from educational exit.
Overall, MCA Math achievement functions as a background risk indicator rather than a sorting mechanism. While lower math performance is associated with elevated disconnection risk, it does not sharply distinguish between marginal employment, broader disconnection, and full detachment, reinforcing the broader finding that academic performance alone is insufficient to explain postsecondary workforce outcomes among non-college graduates.

MCA Reading scores show a consistently weak but statistically significant association with workforce outcomes in each of the five years following exit from formal education. Across all years, higher reading proficiency (levels 3 and 4) is associated with a greater likelihood of meaningful employment (both in-region and statewide), while lower proficiency levels (1 and 2) are associated with a higher probability of having no Minnesota employment record.
However, the magnitude of these differences is modest. Cramer’s V values remain tightly clustered around 0.05 across all five years, indicating that reading proficiency explains only a small portion of the variation in workforce status. Importantly, the pattern is remarkably stable over time: the relationship does not strengthen or weaken as individuals move further from educational exit.
Substantively, these results suggest that while reading proficiency is related to early labor market attachment, it functions more as a background risk factor than a decisive driver. MCA Reading performance differentiates probabilities at the margins but does not sharply sort individuals into attached versus disconnected workforce trajectories.

MCA Science performance shows a statistically detectable but substantively weak relationship with workforce outcomes across all five years after exiting formal education. Cramer’s V values consistently remain around 0.04–0.05, indicating that science proficiency explains only a very small share of variation in post-exit workforce categorization.
Across all years, higher MCA Science levels (levels 3 and 4) are modestly associated with greater likelihood of meaningful employment, particularly Meaningful Employment in Minnesota, while lower scores (levels 1 and 2) are somewhat more concentrated among individuals with No Minnesota employment record. However, these gradients are shallow and overlap heavily across categories.
Importantly, the pattern is stable over time. The strength of association does not meaningfully increase or decrease from year 1 through year 5, suggesting that MCA Science performance does not become more salient as individuals move further from educational exit.
Overall, MCA Science—like MCA Math and Reading—functions as a weak stratifier rather than a driver of early workforce trajectories. While academic proficiency in science is directionally aligned with stronger labor force attachment, it does not meaningfully distinguish between marginal employment, disconnection, or full detachment once individuals leave formal education.

Post-secondary attendance is the single strongest predictor of workforce outcomes in the analysis to date. Across all five years after exiting formal education, whether an individual ever attended post-secondary education is strongly and consistently associated with labor force attachment.
Individuals who attended post-secondary education (but did not graduate) are substantially more likely to be in meaningful employment, both in-region and statewide, and far less likely to have no Minnesota employment record. In year 1, non-attenders are nearly twice as likely to have no MN employment record compared to attenders (31% vs. 19%), and this gap persists through year 5 (37% vs. 27%).
While the strength of association gradually declines over time, it remains substantively large even five years after exit (Cramer’s V = 0.130). This attenuation reflects some convergence in outcomes, but not elimination of the initial advantage associated with post-secondary exposure.
Notably, post-secondary attendance does not simply shift individuals from disconnection to marginal employment—it is associated with clear movement into meaningful employment categories, particularly Meaningful Employment in Minnesota, across all years.
Substantively, these results indicate that post-secondary exposure itself—independent of completion—functions as a powerful anchoring mechanism in early labor market trajectories. Compared to demographics, high school characteristics, or academic performance, post-secondary attendance exerts a larger and more durable influence on workforce attachment, reinforcing its central role in preventing persistent labor force disconnection.

Big-Picture Synthesis: What Actually Matters for Early Workforce Outcomes
This analysis examined four groups of predictors—Demographics, High School Characteristics, High School Academics, and Post-secondary Attendance—to understand how strongly each is associated with workforce outcomes in the five years after exiting formal education.
Below is a structured synthesis that cuts through the noise and focuses on signal strength, consistency over time, and substantive meaning.

1. Demographics: Statistically Present, Substantively Thin
Across all demographic variables, associations with workforce outcomes are consistently weak. While many results are statistically significant due to large sample sizes, effect sizes are small and do not meaningfully differentiate workforce trajectories.
Demographics do not explain why individuals end up in meaningful employment versus marginal attachment or full disconnection. Importantly, these effects also do not grow over time, indicating that early demographic differences do not compound into stronger labor market divergence within the first five years.
Bottom line: Demographics describe populations, but they do not drive workforce outcomes.


2. High School Characteristics: Marginal Sorting, Not Trajectory Control
High school characteristics (e.g., program participation, structural features) show slightly stronger signals than demographics, but still remain weak overall. These variables modestly shift probabilities between meaningful employment and disconnection, but they do not fundamentally alter trajectories.
The most notable pattern is risk buffering rather than outcome transformation: certain characteristics slightly reduce the likelihood of having no MN employment record, but do not reliably move individuals into high-quality employment.
Bottom line: High school characteristics can nudge outcomes at the margins, but they do not anchor workforce attachment.


3. High School Academics: Real Signal, Clear Ceiling
Academic variables (ACT participation and scores, MCA Math/Reading/Science, PSEO, CTE participation and intensity) consistently outperform demographics and general school characteristics. However, their effects remain bounded.
Key patterns across this block: - Higher academic achievement is associated with lower rates of full disconnection - Differences are more pronounced between Meaningful employment vs. No MN record than between meaningful and marginal employment - Effect sizes are stable but do not increase with time - Academic strength alone does not guarantee meaningful workforce attachment
Even the strongest academic signals (ACT Composite, ACT-taking, PSEO participation) plateau at weak-to-moderate association levels.
Bottom line: Academic preparation helps, but it does not determine workforce outcomes on its own.


4. Post-secondary Attendance: The Structural Break
Post-secondary attendance—even without completion—is categorically different from every other predictor examined.
Across all five years: - It has the largest effect size in the entire analysis - It consistently increases the likelihood of meaningful employment - It substantially reduces the risk of no MN employment record - Its influence persists, though it gradually attenuates over time
This variable is not merely predictive; it reorganizes workforce trajectories. Unlike academic or demographic factors, post-secondary attendance acts as an institutional bridge into the labor market.
Importantly, this effect holds even though many attenders do not complete a credential.
Bottom line: Post-secondary exposure is the single most important differentiator of early workforce outcomes.


Core Takeaways

Most commonly cited predictors are weak.
Demographics, school characteristics, and even academic performance explain surprisingly little on their own.
Academic strength matters—but only up to a point.
High achievement reduces risk but does not reliably produce strong labor market attachment.
Workforce disconnection is not primarily an academic failure.
Many disconnected individuals have academic profiles similar to marginally or meaningfully employed peers.
Post-secondary attendance is the inflection point.
It is the only factor that consistently and substantially reshapes workforce outcomes across time.
The policy-relevant distinction is exposure, not completion.
Access to post-secondary systems—not just credentials—appears to be doing critical structural work.



One-Sentence Synthesis

Early workforce outcomes are weakly shaped by who students are and how they perform in high school, but strongly shaped by whether they ever cross into post-secondary education, even briefly.

If you want, the next logical step is to reframe disconnection as a systems-access problem rather than a preparation problem—but I’ll stop here unless you ask.

title: Deeper-Dive Analysis Framework: Non-College Graduates Without Meaningful Workforce Participation
text:
1. Demographics
Demographic variables show statistically significant but generally modest relationships with workforce outcomes across all five years.
Economic status, race/ethnicity, and special education status are all associated with workforce category distributions, but effect sizes are small for race/ethnicity and economic status (Cramer’s V typically ~0.04–0.07). These variables modestly differentiate meaningful employment from marginal employment, but they do not sharply distinguish persistent disconnection from weak attachment.
Special education status stands out within this group. Across all five years, individuals with special education status are consistently overrepresented among those with no Minnesota employment record and underrepresented in meaningful employment categories. While still not determinative on its own, special education status shows the strongest and most stable demographic signal related to persistent disconnection.
Importantly, demographic variables alone do not explain why some individuals remain persistently disconnected while others establish durable workforce attachment. They appear to shape risk, not destiny.

title: Deeper-Dive Analysis Framework: Non-College Graduates Without Meaningful Workforce Participation
text:
2. High School Characteristics
High school and place-based characteristics show very weak relationships with workforce outcomes.
District rurality (Dem_Desc) is statistically associated with workforce categories across all five years, but effect sizes are small and patterns are gradual rather than decisive. Individuals from entirely rural districts show slightly higher in-region employment and slightly lower out-of-state detachment, but differences narrow over time and do not clearly separate persistently disconnected individuals from others.
County-level labor market conditions—average unemployment rates and average wages as a percent of the state average—explain less than 1% of total variance in outcomes. While ANOVA results are statistically significant due to large sample size, differences in mean unemployment or wage context across workforce categories are trivial in magnitude and highly stable over time.
These findings strongly indicate that persistent workforce disconnection is not primarily a local labor market problem. Place matters marginally, but it does not drive long-term detachment.

title: Deeper-Dive Analysis Framework: Non-College Graduates Without Meaningful Workforce Participation
text:
3. High School Academics
High school academic variables show the clearest and most consistent differentiation across workforce outcomes.
Participation in PSEO, taking the ACT, CTE achievement, number of CTE courses taken, ACT composite scores, and MCA scores (math, reading, science) all display statistically significant relationships with workforce categories across all five years.
Several consistent patterns emerge: - Individuals with stronger academic indicators are more likely to be in meaningful employment (both in-region and statewide). - Lower academic preparation is associated with higher likelihood of no Minnesota employment record. - These relationships are graded, not binary: higher scores or deeper engagement correspond to progressively stronger attachment.
However, effect sizes remain modest overall. Academic variables differentiate persistent connection vs persistent disconnection more clearly than demographics, but they still do not produce sharp thresholds. Importantly, many individuals with average or even strong academic preparation still experience weak attachment or disconnection, indicating that academic preparation is necessary but not sufficient for durable workforce outcomes.
CTE engagement deserves special note. CTE concentrators consistently show higher rates of meaningful employment and lower rates of out-of-state detachment than non-CTE peers, but the magnitude of this advantage stabilizes after year three rather than expanding.

title: Deeper-Dive Analysis Framework: Non-College Graduates Without Meaningful Workforce Participation
text:
4. Post-Secondary Exposure (attended.ps)
Attendance at any postsecondary institution—even without completion—shows the strongest relationship with workforce outcomes of any variable examined.
Across all five years, individuals who attended postsecondary education are dramatically more likely to be in meaningful employment and far less likely to have no Minnesota employment record. Cramer’s V values (~0.13–0.20) are substantially larger than those observed for demographics, academics, or place-based factors.
Two critical points emerge: - Postsecondary attendance strongly protects against persistent disconnection. - The advantage is evident immediately and remains stable over time rather than compounding.
This suggests that postsecondary exposure functions less as skill accumulation alone and more as a structural connector—linking individuals to networks, credentials, signaling mechanisms, or institutional supports that facilitate labor market attachment.

title: Deeper-Dive Analysis Framework: Non-College Graduates Without Meaningful Workforce Participation
text:
Overall Conclusions

Persistent workforce disconnection is not driven primarily by local labor market conditions. Place-based unemployment and wage context explain very little variation.
Demographics shape risk but do not determine outcomes. Their influence is real but modest, with special education status being the most consequential within this group.
Academic preparation matters, but it does not guarantee connection. Stronger academics improve odds of meaningful employment but do not eliminate disconnection risk.
Postsecondary exposure is the single most powerful differentiator. Even without degree completion, it substantially reduces the likelihood of persistent disconnection and out-of-region labor force exit.
Persistent disconnection appears structurally embedded rather than episodic. Individuals who are disconnected early tend to remain so, and transitions out of disconnection are relatively rare without a major structural intervention (such as postsecondary entry).

Taken together, these findings suggest that policy efforts focused solely on local job creation or general academic improvement will have limited impact on persistent disconnection. Interventions that create early, durable institutional connections—particularly through postsecondary pathways—are most likely to alter long-term workforce trajectories for non-college graduates in Northeast Minnesota.

Key Takeaways from the Ranking

Structural connection beats background: Postsecondary attendance overwhelms all other variables.

Persistent disconnection is not random, but it is not well-explained by any single variable short of postsecondary exposure.

This ranking supports a central conclusion of your analysis:
persistent workforce disconnection is primarily a structural attachment problem, not a local labor market or demographic inevitability.

title: Deeper-Dive Analysis Framework: Non-College Graduates Without Meaningful Workforce Participation
text:
Plain-Language Interpretation and Conclusions
We looked at a wide range of student, school, and post-school characteristics to understand why some non-college graduates stay connected to the local workforce while others remain disconnected or leave the region in the years after high school.

The single biggest takeaway
The strongest factor by far is whether someone had any post-secondary exposure at all.
Even attending for a short time is strongly linked to being more likely to work, and especially to work in Minnesota. Non-college graduates who never attended post-secondary education are much more likely to be persistently disconnected from the workforce or to leave the state entirely.


What matters next (but less)
Academic preparation matters, but it does not determine outcomes on its own.

Students with higher ACT scores or stronger MCA performance are more likely to be meaningfully employed.
Students who took the ACT, participated in PSEO, or completed CTE pathways tend to have better workforce outcomes than those who did not.
These factors help, but they do not protect everyone from long-term disconnection.

In other words: stronger academics increase the odds, but they are not a guarantee.


Who is most at risk
Some groups are clearly at higher risk of long-term disconnection:

Students who received special education services are much more likely to remain disconnected from the workforce across multiple years.
Low-income students are also more likely to struggle, though income alone does not fully explain persistent disconnection.

These patterns are consistent across all five years after leaving school.


What does not explain disconnection very well
Several commonly cited explanations do not do much to explain long-term workforce outcomes:

Local unemployment rates and average wages explain almost none of the differences.
School district rurality (rural vs mixed vs urban) has only a small effect.
Race and ethnicity show statistically detectable differences, but the size of those differences is small compared to education-related factors.

This suggests that persistent disconnection is not mainly driven by local labor market conditions or geography.


What this means overall
Persistent workforce disconnection among non-college graduates in Northeast Minnesota is not random, but it is also not primarily about place.
It is most strongly associated with: - whether young people ever connect to post-secondary systems, and - how well schools support students with weaker academic preparation or additional learning needs during the transition out of high school.
Simply put: > Staying connected to education after high school—even briefly—matters more than where you live or the local job market.


Implication for policy and practice
If the goal is to reduce long-term workforce disconnection: - Improving transitions after high school is likely more effective than focusing only on job availability. - Supports targeted at special education students and academically vulnerable students are critical. - Policies that treat non-college graduates as a single group miss important differences in risk and opportunity.
This analysis points toward connection, transition, and support as the levers that matter most.

title: Deeper-Dive Analysis Framework: Non-College Graduates Without Meaningful Workforce Participation
text:
1. Post-Secondary Exposure (Even Without Completion)
Evidence from analysis - Attending post-secondary education (without completing) is the strongest and most consistent predictor of: - Meaningful employment in-region - Lower likelihood of having no MN employment record - Effect sizes are large and stable across all five years after exit. - This relationship is stronger than most high school academic indicators.
Interpretation Post-secondary exposure appears to function as a protective experience, even when it does not result in a credential.
Intervention levers - Short-term credential and bridge programs - Stackable credentials tied to local employers - Non-credit workforce certificates housed at colleges - “Stop-out” reengagement programs (designed for non-completers) - Career navigation and advising embedded in post-secondary entry points
What this lever realistically affects - Increases likelihood of sustained labor force attachment - Reduces long-term detachment from both region and state - Improves access to job networks and employer signaling

title: Deeper-Dive Analysis Framework: Non-College Graduates Without Meaningful Workforce Participation
text:
2. Special Education Transition Support
Evidence from analysis - Special education status shows one of the strongest associations with: - Persistent disconnection - No MN employment record - Effects are consistent across: - Disconnection persistence - All five post-exit workforce years
Interpretation This is not about academic ability; it is about transition failures between systems.
Intervention levers - Strengthened transition planning (IEP → workforce) - Extended transition services beyond high school exit - Supported employment and job coaching - Employer partnerships specifically designed for transition-age youth - Case-managed pathways rather than self-navigation
What this lever realistically affects - Reduces persistent disconnection - Improves early attachment, which compounds over time - Prevents drift into long-term detachment immediately after exit

title: Deeper-Dive Analysis Framework: Non-College Graduates Without Meaningful Workforce Participation
section: 3. Career and Technical Education (CTE) Depth and Quality
text:
3. Career and Technical Education (CTE) Depth and Quality
Evidence from analysis - CTE concentrators/completers consistently show: - Higher rates of meaningful employment - Lower rates of no MN employment record - Number of CTE courses taken shows modest but consistent gradients.
Interpretation CTE works best when it is deep and connected, not shallow or incidental.
Intervention levers - Incentivize completion-level CTE pathways - Align CTE programs directly with regional labor demand - Expand work-based learning and paid placements - Strengthen employer co-design of CTE curricula - Reduce “CTE sampling” without completion
What this lever realistically affects - Improves probability of early and stable attachment - Supports in-region employment specifically - Acts as an alternative pathway when post-secondary is not pursued

title: Deeper-Dive Analysis Framework: Non-College Graduates Without Meaningful Workforce Participation
section: 4. Academic Performance as a Sorting Mechanism (Not a Fix)
text:
4. Academic Performance as a Sorting Mechanism (Not a Fix)
Evidence from analysis - ACT and MCA scores are associated with workforce outcomes - Effect sizes are modest and stable - Academic measures explain sorting, not change
Interpretation Raising test scores alone will not materially change workforce attachment patterns for this group.
Intervention levers - Use academic indicators for early identification, not remediation-only strategies - Combine academic support with pathway guidance and exposure - Avoid over-investment in test-score-focused workforce policy
What this lever realistically affects - Improves targeting of supports - Helps identify who may need more structured pathways - Does not, by itself, solve disconnection

title: Deeper-Dive Analysis Framework: Non-College Graduates Without Meaningful Workforce Participation
text:
5. Place-Based Labor Market Conditions (Deprioritized Lever)
Evidence from analysis - County unemployment rates explain <1% of variation - County wage levels show trivial differences across categories - Effects are stable and negligible over time
Interpretation Persistent disconnection is not driven by local labor market tightness.
Intervention levers - Avoid over-reliance on: - Job creation alone - Wage growth alone - Generic “economic development” as a workforce solution
What this lever realistically affects - Broad economic health - Not targeted workforce reattachment for this population

title: Deeper-Dive Analysis Framework: Non-College Graduates Without Meaningful Workforce Participation
text:
Strategic Takeaway
The strongest levers are pathway-based, not place-based.
The most promising interventions: - Increase exposure to post-secondary systems (even without completion) - Strengthen transition supports for special education students - Deepen and align CTE pathways with regional employers
Efforts focused solely on labor market conditions or generalized economic growth are unlikely to meaningfully reduce persistent workforce disconnection among non-college graduates.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
Postsecondary Graduation Location (ps.grad.location)
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between location of postsecondary graduation and post‑graduation outcomes across all timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(9) = 2713.62, Cramer’s V = 0.197, p < .001, N = 23,341【772†source】

5 years after graduation: χ²(9) = 3699.62, Cramer’s V = 0.207, p < .001, N = 28,840【773†source】

10 years after graduation: χ²(9) = 1609.04, Cramer’s V = 0.164, p < .001, N = 19,827【774†source】

The association is moderate in years 1 and 5 and slightly weaker by year 10. The central divide is that regional PS graduates are consistently more likely to work in the region, while graduates outside MN or at MN institutions outside the region are more likely to pursue statewide or out‑of‑state pathways.
Interpretation Over Time
Year 1: Regional graduates show the strongest immediate tie to local jobs, with 65.8% in regional meaningful employment, compared to 23.8% of non‑graduates, 28.7% of MN graduates outside the region, and 22.0% of graduates outside MN. Non‑graduates are most often disconnected (43.4% “not meaningful” and 25.9% “no record”)【772†source】.
Year 5: Regional graduates remain highly concentrated in regional employment (50.2%), far above MN graduates outside the region (18.3%) or graduates outside MN (20.4%). By contrast, MN graduates outside the region have the highest statewide employment (44.0%), reflecting mobility within the state. Non‑graduates remain more disconnected (28.4% “not meaningful” and 31.0% “no record”)【773†source】.
Year 10: Regional graduates sustain a long‑term edge in local employment (43.1%), while MN graduates outside the region remain more mobile (38.0% in statewide employment). Graduates outside MN have lower regional (20.7%) and statewide (17.8%) employment, with a higher share of disconnection (49.4% “no record”). Non‑graduates remain the weakest group, with only 25.6% regional employment and the highest share of disconnection (36.7% “no record”)【774†source】.
Overall, the evidence shows that regional PS graduation strongly anchors individuals in the local workforce, while graduation outside the region or outside MN promotes mobility and statewide attachment. Non‑graduates remain at the greatest risk of disconnection across all timeframes.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
Highest Credential Level (highest.cred.level)
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between highest credential earned and post‑graduation outcomes across all timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(20) = 25,119.08, Cramer’s V = 0.366, p < .001, N = 46,777【760†source】

5 years after graduation: χ²(20) = 7,371.79, Cramer’s V = 0.231, p < .001, N = 34,683【761†source】

10 years after graduation: χ²(12) = 1,030.86, Cramer’s V = 0.132, p < .001, N = 19,828【762†source】

The association is strong in the first year, moderates by year 5, and weakens further by year 10, though it remains significant. The key distinction is that higher credentials (Bachelor’s or above) delay regional employment but lead to stronger statewide employment later, while lower or mid‑level credentials (Associate, less than Associate) are more tied to early and sustained regional employment.
Interpretation Over Time
Year 1: Students with no college are most likely to be in regional meaningful employment (19.9%), but also heavily represented in disconnection categories (44.2% not meaningful, 30.1% no record). Those with some college or Associate degrees show moderate regional employment (18–19%) but are strongly concentrated in “attending PS” (49–69%). Students pursuing a Bachelor’s or higher overwhelmingly remain in education (86.5%) and show the lowest regional employment (5.7%)【760†source】.
Year 5: Regional meaningful employment peaks among less than Associate (42.3%) and Associate degree earners (36.5%), with some college also relatively strong (29.2%). By contrast, Bachelor’s or higher show lower regional attachment (19.1%) but higher statewide meaningful employment (20.5%). Non‑college individuals still show significant disconnection (27.4% not meaningful, 37.0% no record)【761†source】.
Year 10: The regional advantage of Associate and sub‑Associate credentials remains high (42–43%), while Bachelor’s or higher show stronger statewide employment (27.9%) and lower regional employment (26.5%). Non‑college individuals continue to show the weakest outcomes, with the highest disconnection rates (41.7% no record)【762†source】.
Overall, the evidence shows that mid‑level credentials (Associate and below) strongly anchor individuals in regional employment, while Bachelor’s and above foster statewide mobility and stronger longer‑term outcomes, and no credential consistently yields the weakest employment stability.

Overall Insight
Postsecondary experiences draw a clear line between regional anchoring vs. statewide mobility.
1. Access and completion of postsecondary education lead to broader statewide opportunities and reduced risk of disconnection.
2. Absence of postsecondary pathways results in earlier regional employment but higher long‑term vulnerability.
3. The type, level, and location of postsecondary attainment nuance this divide: regional and 2‑year pathways strengthen local attachment, while higher‑level and out‑of‑region pathways expand opportunities but reduce regional ties.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
Postsecondary Graduation by Institution Sector (ps.grad.InstitutionSector)
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between the sector of postsecondary graduation (4‑year public, 2‑year public, other) and post‑graduation outcomes across all timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(12) = 1313.46, Cramer’s V = 0.138, p < .001, N = 22,962【748†source】

5 years after graduation: χ²(12) = 1181.64, Cramer’s V = 0.152, p < .001, N = 17,154【749†source】

10 years after graduation: χ²(6) = 498.68, Cramer’s V = 0.160, p < .001, N = 9,691【750†source】

The relationship is moderate but consistent, strengthening slightly by year 10. The main divide is between 4‑year and 2‑year graduates, with different propensities toward statewide vs. regional employment.
Interpretation Over Time
Year 1: Almost all graduates remain in postsecondary, but small differences emerge. 2‑year graduates show the highest early regional employment (20.6%), compared to 7.1% among “other” graduates and just 4.5% among 4‑year graduates. Graduates of 4‑year and “other” institutions overwhelmingly remain enrolled (86%+), delaying workforce entry【748†source】.
Year 5: Clearer differences appear. 2‑year graduates lead in regional meaningful employment (40.7%), while 4‑year graduates show higher statewide employment (21.8%). “Other” graduates also lean toward regional work (21.7%). Disconnection rates are somewhat higher among 4‑year graduates, but overall the trend is that 2‑year pathways support stronger early attachment to regional jobs【749†source】.
Year 10: By this point, differences remain. 2‑year graduates sustain the highest regional meaningful employment (45.1%), while 4‑year graduates lean toward statewide meaningful employment (29.5%). “Other” graduates remain in the middle with balanced outcomes. Importantly, no‑record rates are lowest for 2‑year graduates (21.6%), suggesting stronger regional retention. In contrast, 4‑year graduates have higher statewide outcomes but also higher “no record” rates (33.6%)【750†source】.
Overall, institution sector matters: 2‑year graduates show stronger long‑term regional employment, while 4‑year graduates pursue statewide opportunities and are more mobile, and “other” graduates fall between.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
AP Exam Participation
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between AP exam participation and post-graduation outcomes in all three timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(4) = 822.44, Cramer’s V = 0.133, p < .001, N = 46,777【581†source】

5 years after graduation: χ²(4) = 301.32, Cramer’s V = 0.093, p < .001, N = 34,683【582†source】

10 years after graduation: χ²(3) = 113.60, Cramer’s V = 0.076, p < .001, N = 19,828【583†source】

The strength of association is strongest in the first year and declines over time, though remains statistically significant. The primary relationship is that AP exam participants are much more likely to attend postsecondary, while non‑participants are more likely to enter meaningful regional employment.
Interpretation Over Time
1 Year After Graduation: Regional meaningful employment is substantially higher among non‑AP students (16.1% vs. 7.7%), while AP exam participants are much more likely to be in postsecondary (68.8% vs. 45.7%). Disconnection is lower for AP participants (6.7% vs. 12.2%)【581†source】.
5 Years After Graduation: Non‑AP students retain an advantage in regional meaningful employment (27.4% vs. 17.1%), while AP participants show higher rates of statewide meaningful employment (19.8% vs. 14.7%) and continued postsecondary enrollment (23.7% vs. 15.3%). Disconnection rates are similar (~21%)【582†source】.
10 Years After Graduation: Regional meaningful employment remains higher for non‑AP students (29.9% vs. 22.7%). AP participants hold an advantage in statewide meaningful employment (27.0% vs. 18.7%). Disconnection is slightly higher for AP participants (36.0% vs. 32.1%), suggesting some trade‑off in regional attachment over time【583†source】.
Overall, AP exam participation sorts students into pathways favoring education and statewide employment, while non‑participants maintain stronger ties to regional meaningful employment.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
MCA Reading (MCA.R)
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between MCA Reading scores and post‑graduation outcomes in all three timeframes (ANOVA across outcome groups):

1 year after graduation: F(4, 42500) = 689.45, p < .001

5 years after graduation: F(4, 31013) = 119.45, p < .001

10 years after graduation: F(3, 17590) = 237.15, p < .001

The results show a very strong early effect that remains significant over time. The primary pattern is that higher MCA Reading scores are associated with postsecondary enrollment and statewide meaningful employment, while lower scores are more tied to regional meaningful employment or not meaningful/disconnected outcomes.
Interpretation Over Time (Tukey HSD highlights)
Year 1:
- Postsecondary attendees score about +0.26 higher than regional meaningful workers (p < .001).
- Not meaningful (+0.09) and No MN record (+0.14) also score higher than regional meaningful (p ≤ .02).
- Takeaway: regional meaningful employment is linked to lower reading scores, while higher scores track into postsecondary and other categories.
Year 5:
- Postsecondary (+0.21), statewide meaningful (+0.17), and No MN record (+0.08) all score above regional meaningful (p < .001).
- Not meaningful scores slightly below regional meaningful (−0.17, p < .001).
- Takeaway: by five years, regional meaningful employment sits lower on the MCA-R spectrum, while postsecondary and statewide jobs skew higher.
Year 10:
- Statewide meaningful (+0.18) and No MN record (+0.14) are significantly above regional meaningful (p < .001).
- Not meaningful scores considerably lower (−0.25, p < .001).
- Takeaway: a decade out, regional meaningful employment remains tied to lower MCA-R scores, with higher scores concentrated in statewide meaningful employment or outside tracked records.
Overall, MCA Reading reinforces that academic achievement predicts longer-term educational and statewide work pathways, while lower scores are associated with stronger regional attachment but also greater risk of not meaningful outcomes.

Key Findings

The strength of association is very strong in the first year but weakens considerably over time. The primary relationship is that PSEO participants are much more likely to pursue postsecondary education, while non‑participants are more likely to enter meaningful regional employment early on.
Interpretation Over Time
1 Year After Graduation: Regional meaningful employment is higher among non‑PSEO students (18.4%) compared to PSEO participants (12.6%). In contrast, PSEO participants are far more likely to be attending postsecondary (61.8% vs. 33.6%). Disconnection is notably lower among PSEO participants (6.5% vs. 16.2%)【542†source】.
5 Years After Graduation: Regional meaningful employment gaps narrow (28.1% non‑PSEO vs. 25.1% PSEO). Importantly, PSEO participants surpass non‑participants in meaningful employment statewide (18.0% vs. 13.3%). Postsecondary attendance is higher among PSEO students (19.1% vs. 11.9%), while disconnection is lower (18.7% vs. 23.5%)【543†source】.
10 Years After Graduation: Regional meaningful employment is relatively similar (29.7% non‑PSEO vs. 26.8% PSEO). PSEO participants maintain higher statewide meaningful employment (24.0% vs. 16.9%), while disconnection rates are similar (~32%). The long‑term pattern suggests PSEO participants transition from education into statewide meaningful jobs, while non‑participants retain an edge in regional meaningful employment【544†source】.

Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between taking the SAT and post-graduation outcomes in all three timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(4) = 228.74, Cramer’s V = 0.070, p < .001, N = 46,777【595†source】

5 years after graduation: χ²(4) = 188.76, Cramer’s V = 0.074, p < .001, N = 34,683【596†source】

10 years after graduation: χ²(3) = 99.99, Cramer’s V = 0.071, p < .001, N = 19,828【597†source】

The effect sizes are small but consistent. The key pattern is that SAT takers are far more likely to attend postsecondary education, while non‑takers are more likely to enter meaningful employment in the region.
Interpretation Over Time
1 Year After Graduation: SAT takers are overwhelmingly in postsecondary (73.5% vs. 47.3% for non‑takers). Regional meaningful employment is much lower for SAT takers (3.2% vs. 15.5%), while disconnection is also somewhat lower (9.0% vs. 11.7%)【595†source】.
5 Years After Graduation: SAT takers maintain higher postsecondary enrollment (30.1% vs. 15.8%). Regional meaningful employment is still much lower (7.6% vs. 26.8%). Interestingly, SAT takers are slightly more likely to be in meaningful employment statewide (18.2% vs. 15.1%). Disconnection is higher among SAT takers (28.6% vs. 20.9%)【596†source】.
10 Years After Graduation: SAT takers continue to show very low regional meaningful employment (11.5% vs. 29.5%), while statewide meaningful employment is similar (18.6% vs. 19.4%). Disconnection is much higher among SAT takers (55.9% vs. 32.0%)【597†source】.
Overall, SAT participation identifies a small group of students who overwhelmingly pursue postsecondary initially, but long‑term outcomes show weak regional attachment and much higher disconnection, suggesting that SAT takers may be more mobile, pursue opportunities outside the region or state, or leave tracked employment systems altogether.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
MCA Science (MCA.S)
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between MCA Science scores and post‑graduation outcomes in all three timeframes (ANOVA across outcome groups):

1 year after graduation: F(4, 37501) = 544.02, p < .001

5 years after graduation: F(4, 26050) = 160.29, p < .001

10 years after graduation: F(3, 11879) = 81.74, p < .001

The results show a very strong early effect that remains significant through 10 years. The key pattern is that higher MCA Science scores are associated with postsecondary education and statewide meaningful employment, while lower scores are tied to regional meaningful employment or not meaningful outcomes.
Interpretation Over Time (Tukey HSD highlights)
Year 1:
- Postsecondary attendees score substantially higher than regional meaningful (+0.38, p < .001).
- Statewide meaningful (+0.07) also scores higher than regional meaningful (p = .025).
- Not meaningful (−0.07) and No MN record (−0.12) score below postsecondary.
- Takeaway: early on, regional meaningful work is tied to lower MCA-S scores, while education and statewide jobs are tied to higher scores.
Year 5:
- Statewide meaningful (+0.25) and postsecondary (+0.32) are far above regional meaningful (p < .001).
- No MN record (+0.11) is also higher.
- Not meaningful (−0.04) is slightly below regional meaningful (p = .044).
- Takeaway: by 5 years, the gap widens, with statewide and postsecondary pathways clearly tied to higher MCA-S scores, while regional meaningful remains lower.
Year 10:
- Statewide meaningful (+0.27) and No MN record (+0.18) score above regional meaningful (p < .001).
- Not meaningful (−0.31) scores well below regional meaningful (p < .001).
- Takeaway: a decade out, regional meaningful employment remains linked to lower MCA-S scores, while higher scores push students into statewide jobs or out of tracked MN employment.
Overall, MCA Science mirrors the MCA Reading pattern: academic achievement is strongly tied to educational and statewide pathways, while lower achievement is associated with stronger regional attachment or risk of weaker employment outcomes.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
CTE Achievement
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between CTE achievement (Concentrator/Completer, Participant, No CTE) and post‑graduation outcomes across all three timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(8) = 508.14, Cramer’s V = 0.074, p < .001, N = 46,777【663†source】

5 years after graduation: χ²(8) = 307.50, Cramer’s V = 0.067, p < .001, N = 34,683【664†source】

10 years after graduation: χ²(6) = 174.53, Cramer’s V = 0.066, p < .001, N = 19,828【665†source】

The associations are modest but consistent. The clearest relationship is that CTE Concentrators/Completers are more likely to enter meaningful employment in the region, while students with no CTE are more likely to be in postsecondary or outside regional attachment.
Interpretation Over Time
1 Year After Graduation: Regional meaningful employment is highest for CTE Concentrators/Completers (19.4%), compared to Participants (15.1%) and No CTE students (12.6%). Postsecondary enrollment is much higher among No CTE (51.3%) and Participants (49.2%) than Concentrators/Completers (41.5%). This suggests that CTE pathways steer students more quickly into regional work while non‑CTE students delay employment through postsecondary【663†source】.
5 Years After Graduation: The regional employment gap persists: 31.9% for Concentrators/Completers vs. 27.2% for Participants and 22.9% for No CTE. Postsecondary attendance is relatively low across all groups (13–17%), but still higher for those without CTE. Concentrators/Completers maintain stronger local employment connections, while non‑CTE students lean slightly more toward statewide employment (15.7%)【664†source】.
10 Years After Graduation: Regional meaningful employment remains strongest among Concentrators/Completers (34.6%), compared to Participants (29.1%) and No CTE students (25.5%). Statewide meaningful employment is more evenly distributed, while disconnection is highest among those with No CTE (35.5%). The long‑term pattern confirms that CTE achievement reinforces regional employment pathways, while students outside CTE are more likely to leave the region or experience disconnection【665†source】.
Overall, CTE achievement consistently predicts stronger regional workforce attachment, distinguishing Concentrators/Completers as the group most likely to remain engaged in meaningful employment within the region over time.

title: Model-Ready Variable Recommendations
text:
As we move from descriptive analysis to predictive modeling, the goal is to retain the strongest predictors while removing weaker or redundant ones.
Below is a structured list by section.



Keep / Prioritize
- SpecialEd Status (strongest demographic predictor)
- Race/Ethnicity (moderate strength, important equity covariate)
Drop / Deprioritize
- Gender (weak, V ≈ .05–.10, fades over time)
- English Learner (very weak, V < .07, small group sizes)
- Economic Status (moderate but weaker compared to later predictors; may retain as a control if needed)




Keep / Prioritize
- Dem_Desc (Rural/Urban) – moderate, useful contextual control
- Avg. Unemployment – strong early F-values, local context matters
- Avg. Wages % State – strong F-values, economic environment indicator
Drop / Deprioritize
- Range School (very weak effect, V ≈ .03–.05)




Keep / Prioritize
- ACT (took ACT, ACT Composite Score) – strong, differentiates pathways
- MCA (Math strongest, Reading & Science secondary) – critical academic predictors
- CTE Achievement – anchors to regional meaningful employment
- Total CTE Courses Taken – consistent predictor of regional attachment
- PSEO Participation – strong early differentiator of statewide vs regional pathways
Drop / Deprioritize
- SAT Taken (consistently weak, V ≈ .07, redundant with ACT)
- AP Exam (moderate, but less powerful than ACT/MCA; may be dropped if multicollinearity is high)




Keep / Prioritize
- Attended Postsecondary Within First Year – strongest early effect (V > .5)
- Ever Attended Postsecondary – very strong differentiator (V > .6)
- Postsecondary Graduation – critical predictor of long-term stability
- Highest Credential Level – strong differentiator between statewide vs regional pathways
- Graduation Location – strong anchor for regional vs statewide attachment
Drop / Deprioritize
- Institution Sector – moderate only (V ≈ .14–.16); may be redundant with credential level & location





Drop: Gender, English Learner, Range School, SAT Taken, possibly AP Exam, possibly Institution Sector

Keep: All others, with focus on SpecialEd, Race/Ethnicity, local economic indicators, ACT/MCA, CTE, and Postsecondary attendance/graduation/credentials.

This balances parsimony (leaner model) with coverage (keeping conceptually important drivers of outcomes).

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
Average County Unemployment Rate (Sophomore–Senior Years)
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between the county unemployment rate during high school and post‑graduation outcomes in all three timeframes (ANOVA on unemployment rate across outcome groups):

1 year after graduation: F(4, 46772) = 12.55, p < .001

5 years after graduation: F(4, 34678) = 13.03, p < .001

10 years after graduation: F(3, 19745) = 9.69, p < .001

Effects are modest but reliable across years.
Interpretation Over Time (Tukey HSD highlights)
Year 1:
- Attending postsecondary comes from higher‑unemployment counties than Meaningful employment in the region (Δ = +0.118, p < .001).
- Not meaningful and No MN record are also higher than Meaningful region (Δ ≈ +0.07 to +0.08, both p < .05).
- Takeaway: in the first year, regional meaningful employment is associated with comparatively lower local unemployment than several alternative pathways.
Year 5:
- Meaningful MN (statewide) > Meaningful region (Δ = +0.146, p < .001).
- Attending ps and No MN record are lower than Meaningful MN (Δ ≈ −0.091 and −0.088, both p ≤ .004).
- Takeaway: by five years out, statewide meaningful employment is associated with higher‑unemployment counties than regional meaningful jobs, while continued schooling and no record skew lower than statewide meaningful.
Year 10:
- Meaningful MN > Meaningful region (Δ = +0.088, p = .0009).
- Not meaningful > Meaningful region (Δ = +0.067, p = .022).
- No MN record < Meaningful MN and < Not meaningful (Δ = −0.103 and −0.082; p ≤ .002).
- Takeaway: a decade out, regional meaningful employment remains linked to lower unemployment contexts than statewide meaningful and not meaningful routes; those with no MN record tend to come from lower‑unemployment counties than peers in statewide/not‑meaningful outcomes.
Overall, the pattern suggests that students from lower‑unemployment counties are more likely to land in meaningful employment within the region, whereas higher‑unemployment origins are more often associated with statewide meaningful, not meaningful, or continued schooling pathways.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
Range School Context
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between attending a Range school and post-graduation outcomes in all three timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(4) = 173.72, Cramer’s V = 0.061, p < .001, N = 46,777【487†source】

5 years after graduation: χ²(4) = 63.68, Cramer’s V = 0.043, p < .001, N = 34,683【488†source】

10 years after graduation: χ²(3) = 57.03, Cramer’s V = 0.054, p < .001, N = 19,828【489†source】

The strength of association is weak overall but consistent. The primary relationship is that Range school students are more likely to achieve meaningful employment in the region compared to non‑Range peers, though differences in postsecondary attendance and disconnection are modest.
Interpretation Over Time
1 Year After Graduation: Regional meaningful employment is slightly higher among Range school students (16.6% vs. 15.0%). Range students are also somewhat more likely to be attending postsecondary (52.1% vs. 46.6%) and less likely to be in not meaningful work (17.8% vs. 21.8%). Disconnection is lower for Range students (10.2% vs. 12.1%)【487†source】.
5 Years After Graduation: Regional meaningful employment advantages grow, with 29.3% of Range graduates employed in the region compared to 25.8% of non‑Range peers. Postsecondary enrollment remains somewhat higher (17.3% vs. 15.7%), while not meaningful and disconnection outcomes are slightly lower for Range graduates (19.6% vs. 21.7% and 19.3% vs. 21.5%)【488†source】.
10 Years After Graduation: The gap in regional meaningful employment becomes more pronounced: 34.0% of Range graduates vs. 28.0% of non‑Range graduates. Range graduates maintain comparable statewide meaningful employment (18.4% vs. 19.7%), and their disconnection remains modestly lower (29.7% vs. 33.1%)【489†source】. The long‑term trend indicates that Range school students are more attached to regional meaningful work than non‑Range peers.

title: Pathways After High School – Northeast Minnesota
text:
This one-page overview integrates effect size tables, key insights, and a visual comparison chart across all four major sections of analysis.




Demographics
- Strongest predictor: SpecialEd Status (V = 0.258, Yr 1).
- Demographics fade in importance over time; SpecialEd and Race/Ethnicity remain the most relevant.
High School Characteristics
- Local economic conditions (unemployment, wages) significantly shape early outcomes (F = 53.1 for unemployment, Yr 1).
- Rural/urban divides also matter, but effects diminish by Year 10.
High School Accomplishments
- Academic/college-prep measures (ACT, MCA, PSEO, AP) → statewide pathways, less regional attachment.
- CTE achievement and course load → strongest predictors of regional meaningful employment.
- MCA Math has the largest overall predictive power (F = 1344.5, Yr 1).
Postsecondary Experiences
- The most powerful overall predictors.
- Attendance and graduation separate students into statewide vs. regional pathways.
- Credential level and location nuance outcomes: regional/2-year credentials anchor locally, 4-year/out-of-state expand mobility.







Effect Sizes Overview







Regional meaningful employment is most strongly tied to CTE in high school and regional/2-year postsecondary pathways.

Statewide employment and mobility stem from academic success and 4-year/out-of-state credentials.

Disconnection is concentrated among non-attenders, non-graduates, and those with weaker preparation, amplified by local economic stressors.

This highlights a dual pathway model:
1. Academic + 4-year trajectories → statewide mobility and higher credentials.
2. CTE + regional PS pathways → strong anchoring in the local workforce.
Both are vital in shaping Northeast Minnesota’s labor market outcomes.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
Special Education Status
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between Special Education status and post-graduation outcomes in all three timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(4) = 3110.70, Cramer’s V = 0.258, p < .001, N = 46,777

5 years after graduation: χ²(4) = 829.87, Cramer’s V = 0.155, p < .001, N = 34,683

10 years after graduation: χ²(3) = 231.15, Cramer’s V = 0.108, p < .001, N = 19,828

The strength of association is strongest in the first year and weakens over time, but the relationship remains significant. The primary pattern is that SpecialEd students are less likely to attend postsecondary and more likely to be in not meaningful or disconnected outcomes. While regional meaningful employment is roughly equal at Year 1, by Years 5 and 10 non-SpecialEd students pull ahead in meaningful employment in the region.
Interpretation Over Time
1 Year After Graduation: Regional meaningful employment is nearly the same for SpecialEd (15.6%) and non-SpecialEd (15.3%). The sharpest differences are in education and disconnection: only 21.4% of SpecialEd students are attending postsecondary compared to 52.5% of non-SpecialEd, and 25.1% of SpecialEd students are disconnected compared to 9.3% of non-SpecialEd. This points to an early divergence where SpecialEd students are disproportionately outside of education and tracked employment.
5 Years After Graduation: Gaps in regional meaningful employment begin to open (SpecialEd 24.6% vs. non-SpecialEd 26.8%). SpecialEd students are still much less likely to be in postsecondary (6.8% vs. 17.6%) and more likely to be not meaningful (29.1% vs. 20.0%) or disconnected (30.0% vs. 19.5%). By this stage, non-SpecialEd students strengthen their advantage in both education and regional meaningful jobs.
10 Years After Graduation: The gap in regional meaningful employment widens further (SpecialEd 24.7% vs. non-SpecialEd 29.9%). Non-SpecialEd students are also more likely to be in meaningful employment statewide (20.6% vs. 11.7%). SpecialEd students remain more concentrated in disconnected outcomes (36.9% vs. 31.7%). The long-term trajectory shows that SpecialEd students are less attached to meaningful regional work and face persistent disadvantages in education and quality employment.

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
Summary
Across all three variable groups — demographic characteristics, high school characteristics, and high school accomplishments — the factors most strongly associated with post-secondary attendance are individual-level characteristics, not school- or community-level ones.
Among demographic predictors, special education status and economic disadvantage stand out as the strongest barriers to post-secondary attendance, with gaps of 35 and 22 percentage points respectively. Gender and race/ethnicity are meaningful but secondary, and the race/ethnicity association is likely partially explained by overlap with economic disadvantage — particularly for American Indian students in the region.
High school characteristics contribute very little. District type has a negligible association with attendance, and while local unemployment and wage levels show statistically significant differences, the effect sizes are too small to be practically meaningful. Where a student goes to school matters far less than who that student is and what they do while they are there.
High school accomplishments tell the most differentiated story. PSEO participation is the single strongest predictor across all variables examined, followed closely by academic performance as measured by ACT scores and MCA proficiency in math, reading, and science. CTE engagement runs in the opposite direction — students with deeper CTE involvement are somewhat less likely to attend post-secondary — pointing to a distinct workforce-first orientation among that group that post-secondary attendance alone does not capture.
Taken together, these findings suggest that post-secondary attendance is shaped primarily by preparation and opportunity factors established well before graduation. Students who arrive at their senior year academically prepared, economically stable, and without a special education designation attend post-secondary at substantially higher rates. For students without those advantages, the gap in attendance is large and consistent across multiple measures.

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
Demographics
All four demographic variables show a statistically significant relationship with post-secondary attendance, though effect sizes vary meaningfully across the group.
Special education status shows the strongest association (φ = 0.273). Students without a special education designation attended post-secondary at a rate of 73%, compared to 38% for students with a special education designation — a gap of 35 percentage points. The interpretation of this finding warrants some care, as post-secondary attendance may carry different meaning for special education students depending on individual transition plans and IEP goals.
Economic status is the second strongest predictor (φ = 0.228). Students not identified as economically disadvantaged attended post-secondary at 76%, compared to 54% for those who were — a 22-percentage-point gap. This association is likely intertwined with other demographic factors, particularly race/ethnicity, given the regional concentration of economically disadvantaged students among certain groups.
Race and ethnicity shows a statistically significant but more modest association (V = 0.164). White students had the highest post-secondary attendance rate at 72%, while American Indian students had the lowest at 52%. Other racial and ethnic groups clustered between 57% and 66%. A large “Unknown” category (n = 8,298) attended at 56%, and the non-random nature of that classification warrants caution in interpretation.
Gender shows the smallest effect in this group (φ = 0.121). Female graduates attended post-secondary at a rate of 74%, compared to 62% for male graduates — an 11-percentage-point gap that, while statistically significant, is modest relative to the other demographic predictors.
Taken together, special education status and economic status are the dominant demographic predictors of post-secondary attendance in this cohort. Gender and race/ethnicity are meaningful but secondary. The race/ethnicity association in particular should be interpreted alongside economic status, as overlap between these characteristics may account for a portion of the observed gap.

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
High School Characteristics
Among the three high school characteristic variables examined, district demographic designation shows a statistically significant but negligible association with post-secondary attendance, while the two school-level economic indicators show small but significant differences across attendance groups.
District demographic designation (Cramer’s V = 0.029) is technically statistically significant but the effect size is essentially zero — the weakest association in this entire analysis. Post-secondary attendance rates are nearly identical across school types: 67% for entirely rural districts, 66% for town/rural mix districts, and 69% for urban/town/rural mix districts. For practical purposes, the type of district a student graduates from has no meaningful relationship with whether they attend post-secondary education.
Average local unemployment rate shows a small but statistically significant difference across attendance groups (F = 428.4, p < .001). Students who attended post-secondary came from school districts with an average unemployment rate approximately 0.29 percentage points lower than those who did not attend. While the difference is statistically significant given the large sample size, the magnitude is modest and should be interpreted with caution.
Average local wage as a percentage of the state average also shows a small but statistically significant difference (F = 65.8, p < .001). Students who attended post-secondary came from districts where average wages were about 0.4 percentage points higher relative to the state average compared to non-attendees. As with unemployment rate, the effect is real but small.
Taken together, high school characteristics as measured here contribute very little to explaining post-secondary attendance. The near-zero effect for district type is particularly notable given that geography played a strong role in workforce outcomes in the prior analysis — suggesting that the type of community a student comes from matters more for what happens after post-secondary than for whether they attend in the first place.

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
High School Accomplishments
High school accomplishment variables show the widest range of effect sizes in this analysis, with PSEO participation and academic performance measures standing out as the strongest predictors of post-secondary attendance.
PSEO participation is the strongest predictor in this group (φ = 0.279). Students who participated in PSEO during high school attended post-secondary at a rate of 80%, compared to 53% for non-participants — a 27-percentage-point gap. This is unsurprising given that PSEO students are already enrolled in college coursework while in high school, but the magnitude of the association confirms that PSEO participation is a robust early signal of post-secondary attendance.
ACT Composite Score shows a large and statistically significant difference across attendance groups (F = 739.9, p < .001). Students who attended post-secondary scored approximately 2.0 points higher on the ACT than those who did not. Given that ACT scores are only available for test-takers — a selected population — this association likely understates the true relationship between academic preparation and post-secondary attendance.
The three MCA proficiency scores — math, reading, and science — all show statistically significant differences across attendance groups, with students who attended post-secondary scoring higher on each measure. The estimated differences are 0.35 proficiency levels for math, 0.44 for reading, and 0.39 for science (all p < .001). These are consistent in direction and meaningful in magnitude, reinforcing the broader pattern that academic preparation in high school is closely linked to post-secondary attendance.
CTE achievement level shows a statistically significant but weak association (Cramer’s V = 0.071). Notably, the direction of the relationship is not straightforward — CTE concentrators and completers attended post-secondary at a lower rate (63%) than both CTE participants (70%) and students with no CTE involvement (70%). This likely reflects the vocational orientation of CTE concentrators, many of whom may be pursuing workforce entry directly rather than post-secondary education.
Total CTE courses taken shows a small but statistically significant difference (F = 565.7, p < .001). Students who did not attend post-secondary actually took more CTE courses on average — about 0.54 more courses than those who did attend. This is consistent with the CTE achievement finding and reinforces the interpretation that deeper CTE engagement is associated with a workforce-first pathway rather than post-secondary attendance.
Taken together, academic preparation variables — PSEO participation, ACT scores, and MCA proficiency — are the dominant high school accomplishment predictors of post-secondary attendance. CTE engagement tells a different story: greater CTE involvement is modestly associated with lower post-secondary attendance, suggesting these students are on a distinct trajectory that the post-secondary attendance outcome may not fully capture.
